target.title: SVTS: Scalable Video-to-Speech Synthesis
target.venue: arXiv preprint (no publication venue stated on the supplied first page)

entries.text: SVTS is presented as a simple scalable video-to-speech system with a video-to-spectrogram predictor and a pretrained neural vocoder.
entries.condition: Method contribution; the predictor is a ResNet18 plus conformer and the vocoder is used after spectrogram prediction.

entries.text: The authors characterize video-to-speech as self-supervised because it needs no manual text transcription; training still uses paired video and audio-derived spectrogram targets.
entries.condition: No manual transcription labels; the described predictor is trained against the corresponding real-audio spectrogram and uses a speaker-audio embedding.

entries.text: The visual predictor uses a 3D convolutional stem, 2D ResNet-18, conformer, and linear projection; the conformer varies in depth and width by model size.
entries.condition: Training/evaluation architectures SVTS-S, SVTS-M, and SVTS-L; visual frames are converted to spectrogram-frame predictions.
entries.quote:
ResNet18+conformer network [13, 15], which becomes deeper
and wider for larger datasets and is trained using a combination
of two established comparative losses.

entries.text: SVTS-S, SVTS-M, and SVTS-L have 27.3, 43.1, and 87.6 million parameters, respectively.
entries.condition: Model parameter counts include ResNet, conformer, and projection layer; no dataset-specific condition.
entries.quote: Num. parameters∗ (M) 27.3 43.1 87.6

entries.text: The conformer depth is 6, 12, and 12 blocks for SVTS-S, SVTS-M, and SVTS-L.
entries.condition: Architecture configuration in Table 1.

entries.text: Attention dimensions are 256, 256, and 512 for SVTS-S, SVTS-M, and SVTS-L.
entries.condition: Architecture configuration in Table 1.

entries.text: Attention head counts are 4, 4, and 8 for SVTS-S, SVTS-M, and SVTS-L.
entries.condition: Architecture configuration in Table 1.

entries.text: All three architectures use conformer convolution kernel size 31.
entries.condition: SVTS-S, SVTS-M, and SVTS-L.

entries.text: All three architectures use feedforward dimension 2048.
entries.condition: SVTS-S, SVTS-M, and SVTS-L.

entries.text: The predictor is trained with L1 and spectral-convergence losses; the pretrained speaker encoder is frozen.
entries.condition: Speaker embeddings come from a separately pretrained speaker-verification encoder trained on VoxCeleb, VoxCeleb2, and LibriSpeech; the encoder remains frozen during predictor training.
entries.quote: Note that the speaker encoder is kept frozen

entries.text: For GRID and LRS3, speaker conditioning uses an embedding from a randomly selected audio clip of the same speaker.
entries.condition: This adds a same-speaker audio-reference requirement at inference; whether the reference clip is excluded from the evaluated utterance and how it is sampled reproducibly are not stated.
entries.quote: audio clip from the same speaker

entries.text: LRW speaker embeddings use audio from the corresponding video because the dataset lacks speaker labels.
entries.condition: At LRW evaluation the reference audio is the audio clip paired with the same video, rather than an independently sampled clip; this audio-reference condition can contain the target utterance.
entries.quote: for this corpus we generate the speaker embeddings using the audio clip from the corresponding video

entries.text: Parallel WaveGAN is a pretrained LibriTTS vocoder used only at inference, with the paper specifying 1 million training iterations.
entries.condition: The vocoder converts predicted mel-frequency spectrograms into waveform; its training uses a comparative and adversarial loss combination.
entries.quote:
employ a version pre-trained on LibriTTS [42] for 1 million it-
erations. Note that it is used only at inference time, allowing for
a substantially simpler training procedure than related video-to-
speech works, which train their own vocoder from scratch [16,
37].

entries.text: GRID contains 1,000 unique sentences, 51 words, 33 speakers, and roughly 27 hours of audio-visual speech.
entries.unit: sentences; vocabulary words; speakers; audio-visual hours
entries.condition: GRID benchmark dataset; experiments include seen-speaker and unseen-speaker versions.

entries.text: LRW has around 150 hours of single-word utterances, hundreds of speakers, and a 500-word vocabulary.
entries.value: approximately 150 hours; hundreds of speakers; 500 words
entries.condition: LRW is recorded in the wild with variable lighting, head poses, and background noise; speaker labels are unavailable.

entries.text: LRS3 is described as a 312-hour dataset with more than 50,000 words and thousands of speakers.
entries.value: 312 hours; more than 50,000 words; thousands of speakers
entries.condition: LRS3 benchmark; separate seen-speaker and original unseen-speaker protocols are used.

entries.text: The English-only VoxCeleb2 addition brings LRS3 training data to around 1,550 hours; utterances longer than 24 seconds are excluded from training for both corpora.
entries.unit: combined footage hours; maximum training-utterance duration threshold
entries.condition: LRS3 plus English-only VoxCeleb2 training; the LRS3 validation and test sets are retained for comparison; long-utterance exclusion is stated for training.

entries.text: Mouth crops are derived from 68 facial landmarks detected by RetinaFace and pretrained 2D-FAN; landmarks are averaged over a 12-frame sliding window for alignment.
entries.condition: Visual preprocessing for GRID, LRW, and LRS3.

entries.text: The system crops a 96×96 grayscale mouth region; source video is sampled at 20 fps, and audio is 24 kHz with 80-band log-mels, 2048 frequency bins, 12.5 ms hop, 50 ms Hann window.
entries.unit: pixels; video fps; audio Hz; mel bands; frequency bins; hop ms; window ms
entries.condition: Data preprocessing and spectrogram input/target setup; the supplied text does not report the predictor's feature-normalization statistics.

entries.text: Training augmentation uses random 88×88 crops, horizontal flips at probability 0.5, random erasing at probability 0.5, area 2–33% of a frame, and aspect ratio 0.3–3.3; testing uses center crops of 88×88.
entries.unit: crop pixels; flip probability; erase probability; erased-frame area; aspect ratio
entries.condition: General training augmentation and test-time crop policy.

entries.text: LRS3 training applies one contiguous time mask per second, with each mask length uniformly sampled from 0 to 0.4 seconds.
entries.unit: masks per utterance second; mask duration in seconds
entries.condition: LRS3 experiments only; masked video frames are replaced by the average pixel value.

entries.text: Video is sampled at 20 fps, spectrogram output at 80 frames per second; each video-frame feature is projected to hidden size 320 and reshaped into 4×80 spectrogram frames.
entries.unit: video fps; spectrogram fps; hidden dimensions; mel frames per video frame × mel bands
entries.condition: Predictor temporal rate and output representation.

entries.text: GRID and LRW use AdamW with learning rate 1×10−3, β1=0.9, β2=0.98, weight decay 1×10−2, 10% warmup, then cosine decay.
entries.unit: learning rate; β1; β2; weight decay; warmup fraction of iterations
entries.condition: GRID and LRW predictor training; the paper does not report random seeds or repeated-run counts.

entries.text: LRS3 seen-speaker training uses maximum learning rate 7×10−3; unseen LRS3, including LRS3 plus VoxCeleb2, uses 1×10−3.
entries.unit: maximum learning rate (seen; unseen and combined unseen)
entries.condition: LRS3 seen versus unseen-speaker predictor training.

entries.text: Training lasts 200, 150, 500, and 150 epochs for GRID, LRW, LRS3 seen, and LRS3 unseen, respectively.
entries.unit: epochs (GRID / LRW / LRS3 seen / LRS3 unseen)
entries.condition: Predictor training; the combined LRS3+VoxCeleb2 case is included with the unseen-speaker setting.

entries.text: A checkpoint is saved after each epoch and the final selected checkpoint is the one with the lowest validation loss.
entries.condition: Validation-based model selection; exact validation partition composition is not fully specified for all datasets.

entries.text: Objective evaluation uses PESQ, STOI, ESTOI, and WER.
entries.condition: WER is calculated by applying a pretrained ASR model to generated audio; PESQ/STOI/ESTOI assess speech quality or intelligibility.
entries.quote:
We measure the quality and accuracy of our generated samples
via 4 objective metrics.

entries.text: WER reference transcripts are ASR predictions on the corresponding real audio rather than manual transcripts.
entries.condition: This pseudo-transcription protocol is used to compare generated audio with the paired real audio; text-normalization and ASR decoding details are not reported.
entries.quote:
We propose to forego the use of manual
text transcriptions, and use instead the transcription predicted
from the corresponding real audio as the ground truth.

entries.text: GRID WER uses an ASR model pretrained on LRW, LRS2, and LRS3 and fine-tuned on GRID using the split from [3]; its real-audio test WER is 0.1%.
entries.unit: % WER on real GRID test audio
entries.condition: GRID ASR reference model; adopted GRID split from [3]. ASR decoding and text normalization are not specified.

entries.text: LRW WER uses an ASR model trained only on LRW, with reported real-audio WER 1.68%.
entries.condition: LRW ASR reference model; the exact evaluation partition for the reported ASR error and decoding/text normalization are not given.

entries.text: The authors do not report LRS3 WER because no ASR model was found that accurately recognizes their generated LRS3 samples.
entries.condition: LRS3 results report PESQ, STOI, and ESTOI only; the table reports WER as unavailable.
entries.quote: unable to ﬁnd a speech

entries.text: The authors caution that objective speech metrics do not perfectly correlate with human quality and intelligibility perception and encourage listening to samples.
entries.condition: Applies to reported objective metrics and subjective perceptual judgments.
entries.quote:
widely known that no objective speech metric correlates per-
fectly with human perception of quality and intelligibility [38].
Therefore, we highly encourage readers to listen to the gener-
ated samples available on our project website 6 rather than rely
solely on the reported metrics.

entries.text: The authors claim state-of-the-art results on GRID and LRW and substantially better LRW results than earlier approaches.
entries.condition: Their GRID claim is qualified by the metric- and split-specific results: the unseen-speaker WER is worse than their prior GAN result.
entries.quote: considerably outperform previous approaches on

entries.text: On unseen GRID speakers, SVTS-S improves PESQ, STOI, and ESTOI but loses to the authors' prior GAN in WER.
entries.condition: GRID unseen-speaker setting; see target and comparator rows in Table 2.
entries.quote:
On unseen speakers, our model achieves a better
PESQ, STOI, and ESTOI but is outperformed by our previous
GAN-based work [24] in WER.

entries.text: The authors claim SVTS-M is superior to previous LRW approaches on all reported metrics by a wide margin.
entries.condition: LRW unseen-speaker result; exact table values and baselines are recorded in Table 2 entries.

entries.text: The authors claim to be the first to present intelligible video-to-speech results on LRS3.
entries.condition: LRS3 claim is based on reported PESQ/STOI/ESTOI and the authors' perceptual description; no LRS3 WER is reported.
entries.quote:
To the best of our knowledge, we are the ﬁrst to show
intelligible results on the challenging LRS3 dataset.

entries.text: The authors say adding VoxCeleb2 improves all LRS3 unseen metrics and demonstrates gains from additional, distribution-mismatched training data.
entries.condition: LRS3 validation and test sets remain the same in the combined-data experiment; Table 2 records scores.

entries.text: The authors describe GRID seen outputs as highly realistic and their unseen-speaker outputs as less noisy and voice-profile accurate.
entries.condition: Author perceptual assessment; the paper does not document a formal listener study protocol.

By perceptually evaluating the
generated samples, we ﬁnd that our seen speaker reconstruc-
tion is highly realistic and could be mistaken for real audio.

entries.condition: LRW unseen-speaker assessment; no formal listening-test protocol is reported.

entries.text: The linked ParallelWaveGAN LibriTTS recipe defaults to the clean subset: train-clean-100 plus train-clean-360, dev-clean, and test-clean; it computes normalization statistics from the training split and applies those statistics to train/dev/eval features.

entries.text: The linked LibriTTS vocoder config sets 24 kHz audio, FFT 2048, hop 300 samples, window 1200 samples, Hann window, 80 mels, and mel range 80–7600 Hz; the paper omits the mel-frequency range.

entries.text: The linked speaker-encoder implementation preprocesses audio to 16 kHz, uses 40 mel channels with 25 ms window and 10 ms hop, and normalizes volume toward −30 dBFS; these conditions are not specified in the paper.
entries.unit: sample rate Hz; mel channels; window ms; hop ms; target dBFS
entries.condition: Settings in the linked Real-Time-Voice-Cloning speaker-encoder implementation; the paper identifies the encoder repo but does not enumerate its audio preprocessing settings.

entries.text: The linked encoder inference code averages partial-utterance embeddings and L2-normalizes the result; default partials are 160 mel frames (1.6 s) with 50% overlap.
entries.unit: mel frames per partial; partial duration seconds; overlap
entries.condition: Speaker embedding inference in the linked encoder repository; the paper only says an embedding is extracted from a random audio clip.

entries.text: The linked speaker-encoder preprocessing resamples audio when needed, applies increase-only volume normalization by default, and trims long silence when WebRTC VAD is available; the paper omits these details.
entries.condition: Behavior of the linked speaker-encoder preprocessing function; VAD-based silence trimming is conditional on WebRTC VAD being installed.

entries.text: The linked speaker-encoder preparation code uses LibriSpeech train-other-500, filters VoxCeleb1 to anglophone-nationality speakers, and selects VoxCeleb2 dev/aac for training; the paper does not give these pretraining data-selection details.

questions.q: What information beyond silent video does SVTS require at use time?
questions.answer: It requires a speaker embedding obtained from audio: a random same-speaker audio clip for GRID/LRS3, and the corresponding video's audio for LRW. The paper does not say the GRID/LRS3 reference is disjoint from the evaluated utterance.

questions.q: What are the main reported performance claims, and where does the target lose to a prior system?
questions.answer: The authors claim state-of-the-art GRID results and superiority on all LRW metrics, and report first intelligible LRS3 results. On GRID unseen speakers, SVTS-S is worse than their earlier GAN in WER (17.85% versus 16.12%).

questions.q: Which evaluation conditions are missing and should be qualified in a review?
questions.answer: Seeds/repeated runs, exact or sample-counted test partitions, some speaker-overlap details, validation-set composition for checkpoint selection, feature normalization, ASR decoding/LM/text normalization, chance-level references, and a formal listening-test protocol are unreported.

questions.q: What details become available only from the linked repositories?
questions.answer: The ParallelWaveGAN recipe supplies LibriTTS clean train/dev/test partitions and training-statistics normalization; the linked speaker encoder supplies its 16 kHz/40-mel audio preprocessing, volume normalization, silence trimming, and partial-embedding aggregation.
